identified_elements.generic_description: European-style doublet or tunic with decorative embroidered trim; teal-green outer garment with orange-brown inner layer; white ruffled linen collar; fitted at torso, extending to mid-thigh
identified_elements.confidence_note: The garment is visually consistent with late 16th-century European doublet construction (fitted torso, mid-thigh length, layered sleeves). However, the reference material on colonial Andean dress (Dialnet sources) discusses mantas and camisetas as indigenous garments worn by mulatos, and notes that Spanish doublets were sometimes confused with these indigenous forms. The visual evidence shows a European-cut garment with embroidered trim typical of Spanish fashion, not an Andean manta. No specific colonial term in the reference material precisely matches this particular garment type as depicted.

The reference material repeatedly describes 'cuellos de encaje' (lace collars) as standard dress elements for afrodescendant figures in colonial portraiture. The visual evidence shows a white, ruffled, gathered collar consistent with late 16th-century linen lace collars. This term is well-supported by both visual evidence and period documentation.

The reference material explicitly documents 'zarcillos de oro' (gold earrings) as jewelry worn by afrodescendant figures in colonial portraits. The visual evidence shows circular gold earrings on all three figures. The term is well-attested in period sources and matches the visual evidence.

identified_elements.confidence_note: The reference material describes 'gargantilla' as a necklace worn at the chest by afrodescendant women and men of status. stage_3_narrative.description: Oil on canvas portrait of three adult male figures of African descent, painted by Andrés Sánchez Gallque in 1599. The work is titled 'Los mulatos de Esmeraldas' and is housed in the Museo de América, Madrid (on deposit from the Museo del Prado collection). The painting was sent from the Real Audiencia of Quito to Spain in 1599, commissioned by Juan del Barrio de Sepúlveda, an oidor (judge) of the Real Audiencia. The three figures are arranged in parallel, frontal alignment across the canvas, each occupying approximately one-third of the composition width. All three are depicted as life-size or monumental standing figures facing the viewer at a three-quarter angle. Each figure wears a European-style doublet or tunic with decorative embroidered trim (ribete), a white ruffled linen collar (cuello de encaje), and a multi-strand necklace of white pearls or shells (gargantilla or collar de perlas) worn at the chest. Each wears gold circular earrings (zarcillos de oro). The leftmost figure (fig_01) wears a teal-green outer garment with orange-brown inner layer and holds a spear (lanza) vertically in his left hand and a shield (escudo) in his right hand. The central figure (fig_02) wears a tan-brown outer garment with orange-brown inner layer and holds a spear vertically in his left hand and a helmet or plumed hat (yelmo or sombrero) in his right hand. The rightmost figure (fig_03) wears a green outer garment with orange-yellow inner layer and holds a spear vertically in his left hand and a hat with white plume (sombrero) in his right hand. All three figures hold identical spears with dark metal blades and wooden shafts. The composition is symmetrical and emphasizes collective identity and formal portraiture rather than narrative interaction. The background is neutral beige-gray, and lighting is diffuse and even across all three figures. Three inscribed labels appear above the figures: 'DON PZZAS' (left), 'DON FRAN.DE AROBE. 5 6.A' (center), and 'DÓDOMINGO. 1 6.A' (right). A decorative cartouche in the upper right contains a longer inscription in Spanish: 'Filipinos Catholicos Reglishanos Indiar Dios Doctrinados Auspicera Ant Dios Cancilla Diel Oydor Sus Excelencias Fieles Curante Anno 1599'. The painting combines visual elements from three continents: European clothing and formal portraiture conventions; African martial symbols (the spears with iron points); and Andean indigenous jewelry (collars, earrings, and other ornaments). The work is understood by scholars to employ Western pictorial language to convey to the Spanish king the image of submission to the Crown by a portion of the cimarron (maroon) population. The painting is classified as a colonial civil portrait (retrato civil colonial), a casta portrait (retrato de casta), and a work of the Quiteño school (Escuela quiteña). The scene is terrestrial and exterior, depicting a coastal landscape setting (escena terrestre/exterior - paisaje costero). The figures are secular personages (personajes profanos) depicted as adults (edad: adulto) in a composed scene (escena: compuesta) with a collective character (personaje colectivo). The work addresses themes of racial and cultural mestizaje, cimarronaje (marronage), and vasallaje a la Corona (vassalage to the Crown).

stage_4a_results.agency_reading: Figure fig_01, positioned at the left of the composition, maintains an upright, frontal posture with shoulders squared toward the viewer and a direct, unflinching gaze that meets the eye without deference or avoidance. The figure's body language communicates composure and self-possession: the spine is straight, the head held level, and the bearing dignified rather than submissive or deferential. This postural authority is reinforced by the figure's active grip on a long spear or lance held vertically, a weapon that signals martial capability and agency rather than passivity. The direct frontal presentation, combined with the formal naming inscription above ("DON PZZA'S"), suggests a deliberate assertion of individual identity and status within the pictorial field. In the context of colonial casta painting conventions, where figures of African descent were typically rendered in subordinate poses or domestic labor, this upright stance and commanding gaze constitute a visual claim to self-awareness and a degree of authority that resists the marginalizing logic of the genre itself. The figure's placement alongside two other identically posed and equipped figures, all bearing weapons and formal titles, further suggests a collective assertion of martial or civic standing that transcends the hierarchical racial categories the casta system was designed to enforce.

friction.contested_element: The interpretation of fig_01's upright, frontal posture with squared shoulders, direct gaze, and vertical spear grip as signifying either subordination within a hierarchical system or agency and self-possessed authority.
friction.resolution_note: Both readings accurately describe the same verifiable visual elements: fig_01 stands upright with shoulders squared toward the viewer, maintains a direct forward gaze without downward aversion, holds a spear vertically with a relaxed grip, wears elaborate dress including a pearl collar and gold earrings, and is positioned frontally in the composition with a formal inscribed name above. These elements are visually present and unambiguous. However, the posture itself—upright, frontal, dignified bearing—is not inherently coded as either subordinate or agentic in visual language. The same bodily configuration can be read as: (A) the formal, dignified presentation of a figure within an established social order (subordination reading), or (B) a deliberate assertion of individual identity and martial standing that resists marginalizing conventions (agency reading). The ambiguity cannot be resolved by examining the posture alone, because posture does not carry fixed meaning independent of interpretive framework. What would resolve this: (1) comparative visual evidence showing how casta paintings typically render figures of African descent in subordinate vs. agentic poses, or (2) documentary evidence about the historical status or identity of the named individual, or (3) analysis of the compositional logic and patronage context of this specific work. The image itself contains no internal visual marker that definitively privileges one reading over the other.
